notes.h: The concept of a microbiome
notes.b: Your body, and every patch of soil, is home to huge numbers of tiny organisms that live together rather than alone. Biologists treat that whole community as one thing, called a microbiome.
points: A microbiome is the whole community of microorganisms (bacteria, archaea, fungi, protists and viruses) living together in a particular environment, such as the human gut, the skin or the soil. It is a community of many kinds, not a single species and not just bacteria.
A microbiome also includes the genes of these microorganisms and the products they make.
The organisms themselves are often called the microbiota; many people use the two words for the same thing, so don't be thrown if a question uses either.
A microbiome is an ecological community (different species living and interacting in one place): its members compete, feed on each other's products and interact with their host or surroundings.
The make-up of a microbiome changes with conditions such as food, pH, oxygen, temperature and water, because each species thrives only in certain conditions.
A diverse microbiome, with many species, is generally more stable and recovers better after a disturbance, because if one species is lost others can often do its job.

Most microorganisms are not pathogens (disease-causing): the majority in a healthy microbiome are harmless (commensals, which gain without harming the host) or beneficial (mutualists, where both sides gain). There is more on this in Biotic factors and relationships.
notes.tip: A common slip is to call a microbiome just bacteria, or a single species. Say it is a community of many kinds of microorganisms.

notes.h: Studying microbiomes by sequencing DNA
notes.b: A microbiome is hard to study because you can't simply grow its members in a dish. Scientists read the DNA of the whole community at once instead.
points: Most of these microorganisms cannot be grown on agar (the jelly used to culture microbes in the laboratory), so culturing would miss most of the community.
Microbiomes are therefore studied mainly by extracting all the DNA from a sample, e.g. faeces or soil.
The extracted DNA is sequenced to identify which organisms and genes are present, so the community can be described without growing any of it. There is more on this in DNA sequencing.

notes.h: The human microbiome: where it lives and how big it is
notes.b: Humans are not microbe-free. Several parts of the body carry their own microbiomes, and the biggest by far is in the gut.
points: Humans carry microbiomes in the gut, mouth, nose, skin and vagina.

The largest is in the gut, and most of the gut's microorganisms live in the large intestine (colon), where food moves slowly and there is almost no oxygen, so most are anaerobic bacteria (bacteria that live without oxygen).
A 2016 estimate found that the body contains about as many bacterial cells (about 38 trillion) as human cells (about 30 trillion), a ratio of roughly 1 : 1.
The older, often-quoted figure of ten bacteria for every human cell is now thought to be an overestimate.
The gut contains hundreds of species, and each person's combination is different.
notes.tip: Put most gut microorganisms in the large intestine, not the stomach (too acidic) or the small intestine. Quote the 1 : 1 ratio, because the 10 : 1 figure is out of date.

notes.h: How a baby acquires its microbiome
notes.b: A baby starts life with almost no microbiome and builds one from its first contacts. How it is born and fed shapes which microorganisms arrive first.
points: A baby's gut is colonised (first settled by microorganisms) at birth and soon after.
Babies born vaginally pick up microorganisms from the mother's vagina and gut.
Babies born by caesarean section are first colonised mostly by skin and hospital microorganisms, so their early gut microbiome is different.
Breast milk contains sugars (oligosaccharides) that the baby cannot digest but that feed beneficial gut bacteria such as Bifidobacterium.
The microbiome changes with diet, weaning (the switch from milk to solid food), antibiotics, environment (e.g. pets, farm animals, siblings) and age, becoming more stable in childhood.
The host provides a warm, moist, food-rich, stable home, and the microorganisms provide digestion, vitamins and protection.
This mutualism (a relationship in which both partners benefit) is an example of how organisms depend on each other.

notes.h: The gut microbiome and digestion: fermenting fibre
notes.b: Humans can't digest everything they eat, but gut bacteria can. They turn part of our undigested food into useful products.
points: Human enzymes cannot digest dietary fibre, e.g. cellulose and other plant cell-wall polysaccharides, and resistant starch, so it reaches the large intestine undigested.
There, gut bacteria ferment the fibre anaerobically (break it down without oxygen), using their own enzymes.
The main products of fermentation are short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): acetate, propionate and butyrate.
The colon absorbs the SCFAs: butyrate is the main energy source of the cells lining the colon, which keeps the lining healthy.
The other SCFAs are carried to the liver and body cells and used for energy.
Gases, namely CO₂, hydrogen and, in some people, methane made by archaea, are by-products of fermentation.
notes.tip: Gut bacteria ferment fibre; humans do not digest it. Never write that humans digest cellulose.

notes.h: The gut microbiome and digestion: vitamins and other help
notes.b: Fermentation is not the only service gut bacteria provide. They also make vitamins and handle substances our own enzymes can't.
points: Gut bacteria make vitamin K, needed for blood clotting, and some B vitamins, part of which the body absorbs.
Gut bacteria also break down some substances that human enzymes cannot, e.g. some plant chemicals and some drugs.
Gut bacteria convert bile salts (made by the liver to help digest fats), which affects how fats are absorbed.
Herbivores depend even more on their microbiome: cattle, sheep and rabbits rely on microorganisms to digest cellulose, which their own enzymes cannot do.
The large intestine, where most of this happens, also absorbs water from the remaining food. There is more on this in The Digestive System.
notes.tip: Exams have asked for two beneficial functions of the bacteria in the digestive tract. Choose from vitamin production, digestion, competition with pathogens and benefit to the immune system, and give each in a short phrase.

notes.h: The gut microbiome and protection against pathogens
notes.b: A gut full of harmless bacteria leaves little room for invaders. This crowding-out effect protects the host and is called colonisation resistance.
points: Protection against pathogens is called colonisation resistance: the normal gut microbiota occupy the space and attachment sites on the gut lining and use up the nutrients that pathogens would need.
Some gut microorganisms make acids that lower the pH, and some make antibacterial proteins (bacteriocins) that kill competing bacteria.
The skin and vaginal microbiota protect in the same way.
In the vagina, Lactobacillus bacteria make lactic acid, keeping the pH low, which stops many pathogens growing. There is more on this in Innate and adaptive immunity.
notes.tip: Competition with pathogens is a standard answer on the benefits of gut bacteria. Name how they compete: space, nutrients, acid or bacteriocins.

notes.h: When antibiotics disturb the gut microbiome
notes.b: Colonisation resistance only works while the normal bacteria are present. If they are wiped out, harmful microorganisms can move in.
points: When antibiotics kill many normal gut bacteria, pathogens can take over: e.g. the bacterium Clostridioides difficile can multiply and cause severe diarrhoea.
The yeast Candida can also overgrow when the normal microbiota are reduced, causing thrush. There is more on this in Pathogens.
Repeated C. difficile infection can be treated by faecal microbiota transplant, which restores a healthy microbiome from a donor.

notes.h: The gut microbiome and immune signalling
notes.b: The gut microbiome also talks to the immune system. Chemical signals from the microorganisms help the body learn what to attack and what to ignore.
points: The gut wall contains a large part of the body's immune tissue, so the microorganisms are in constant contact with immune cells.
Molecules from gut microorganisms, e.g. parts of their cell walls and SCFAs such as butyrate, are detected by immune cells in the gut lining, which then send signals.
In early life these signals 'train' the immune system to tolerate harmless microorganisms and food while still responding to pathogens.
E.g. butyrate promotes suppressor T cells (also called regulatory T cells), which damp down inflammation. There is more on this in White blood cells.
notes.tip: For the immune benefit of gut bacteria, say their signals train the immune system to tolerate harmless microorganisms and food but still respond to pathogens.

notes.h: The gut barrier, evidence and limits
notes.b: The microbiome also helps keep the gut wall intact. Evidence for its role in immunity is real, but much of it shows links rather than proof of cause.
points: The microbiome helps maintain the gut barrier: it stimulates the lining to make mucus and keeps its cells tightly joined.
This stops bacteria and their products leaking into the blood and triggering inflammation.
Germ-free mice, raised completely free of microorganisms, have poorly developed gut immune tissue, which suggests the microbiome is needed for normal immune development.

A less diverse or altered gut microbiome has been linked to inflammatory bowel disease, allergies, asthma and some autoimmune diseases (where the immune system attacks the body's own cells), which fits the hygiene hypothesis. There is more on this in Emerging diseases and society.
These links are mostly correlations: it is often not known whether the altered microbiome causes the disease or results from it.
notes.tip: Links between the microbiome and disease are mostly correlations, so don't state them as proven causes. Say 'is linked to' rather than 'causes'.

notes.h: The gut microbiome and metabolic health
notes.b: Metabolic health is about how the body handles energy. The gut microbiome influences it in three main ways.
points: Metabolic health means healthy body mass, blood glucose, blood fats and blood pressure, without obesity or type 2 diabetes.
First, it affects how much energy is extracted from food: more efficient fermentation of fibre releases more energy as SCFAs.
Second, signals from SCFAs affect appetite hormones and how the body stores fat and controls blood glucose.

Third, inflammation from a leaky gut barrier (one that lets bacteria and their products into the blood) is linked to insulin resistance, where cells respond poorly to insulin and blood glucose stays high.

notes.h: Metabolic health: evidence and diet
notes.b: Animal experiments suggest the microbiome can affect body fat, but human evidence is weaker. Diet is a major factor in shaping the microbiome itself.
points: In a 2006 study, germ-free mice given gut microorganisms from obese mice gained more body fat than germ-free mice given microorganisms from lean mice, on the same diet.
This shows the microbiome can affect fat storage, at least in mice, because diet was the same in both groups.
In humans, people with obesity or type 2 diabetes often have a less diverse gut microbiome, but this is a correlation, partly explained by differences in diet.
A diet high in varied fibre from vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains feeds fibre-fermenting bacteria and is linked to a more diverse microbiome and more SCFAs.
A diet high in sugar, fat and processed food and low in fibre is linked to lower diversity.
notes.tip: The links to obesity and diabetes in people are correlations, not proven causes. Don't make claims about the gut-brain axis or mental health.

notes.h: Dysbiosis and looking after the microbiome
notes.b: A healthy microbiome is balanced, and that balance can be lost. Some everyday habits protect it.
points: Dysbiosis is an imbalance in the microbiome, e.g. a loss of diversity or of beneficial species, or overgrowth of harmful ones.
Causes of dysbiosis include antibiotics, which kill beneficial as well as harmful bacteria, a low-fibre diet, infection, stress and some medicines.
Eat plenty of varied fibre to promote a healthy gut microbiome, because fibre feeds the fermenting bacteria.
Eat fermented foods containing live microorganisms, e.g. live yogurt or kefir.
Take antibiotics only when needed and complete the course as prescribed; this also reduces antibiotic resistance. There is more on this in Emergence and spread of infectious disease.

notes.h: Probiotics and prebiotics
notes.b: Two similar-sounding words describe two different ways of supporting gut bacteria: adding live microorganisms, or feeding the ones already there.
points: Probiotics are live microorganisms taken in food or supplements, e.g. Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species, to benefit health.
Prebiotics are food components that humans cannot digest but that feed beneficial gut bacteria, e.g. some fibres in onions, garlic, leeks, bananas and oats.
Evidence that probiotics help is good for some conditions, e.g. reducing diarrhoea caused by antibiotics, but weak or mixed for many claims.
Most probiotics do not permanently change the microbiome.
notes.tip: Don't mix them up: probiotics are the live microorganisms, prebiotics are the food for them.

notes.h: The soil microbiome: scale and the carbon cycle
notes.b: Soil is one of the richest microbial habitats. Its microorganisms cycle many nutrients, and carbon is the first example.
points: A single gram of fertile soil can contain hundreds of millions to billions of bacteria, many metres of fungal hyphae (thread-like fungal filaments) and thousands of species.
Together these microorganisms cycle many nutrients, not just one.
Carbon: bacteria and fungi decompose dead plants, animals and dung, respiring the organic carbon and releasing CO₂.
Part of the dead matter is turned into stable humus, which stores carbon in the soil for many years. There is more on this in The carbon cycle.
Fungi are the main decomposers of wood and of the tough lignin and cellulose of dead plants.

notes.h: The soil microbiome: the nitrogen cycle
notes.b: Plants need nitrogen in a form they can absorb, and soil microorganisms supply it at several steps.
points: Decomposers release ammonium from proteins in dead matter.
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, both free-living and in legume root nodules, add nitrogen from the air.
Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate, the main form plants absorb.
Denitrifying bacteria in waterlogged soils convert nitrate back to nitrogen gas, and some nitrous oxide, N₂O, is released. There is more on this in The nitrogen cycle.
notes.tip: Name what each group of microorganisms does, not which species they are; names of nitrogen-cycle organisms are not required.

notes.h: The soil microbiome: phosphorus, sulfur and methane
notes.b: Soil microorganisms also free up phosphorus and sulfur for plants, and they control whether soil gives off or takes up methane.
points: Phosphorus: some soil bacteria and fungi release phosphate from organic matter and from insoluble minerals.
Mycorrhizal fungi (fungi living in partnership with plant roots) carry phosphate and water to plant roots in exchange for sugars. There is more on this in Biotic factors and relationships.
Sulfur: decomposers release sulfur from proteins as sulfate, which plants absorb.
Methane: in waterlogged soils and bogs, where there is no oxygen, methane-producing archaea release methane.
In drier, aerated soils other bacteria oxidise methane, so soils can be a source or a sink of methane.

notes.h: The soil microbiome: other roles
notes.b: Beyond cycling nutrients, soil microorganisms shape the soil itself and affect how well plants grow. Farming methods can help or harm them.
points: Soil structure: fungal hyphae bind soil particles together, and bacteria make sticky polysaccharides, forming crumbs, called aggregates, with air spaces between them.
This structure improves drainage and aeration and reduces erosion.
A healthy, diverse soil microbiome suppresses some plant diseases, by competition and by antibiotic production.
Some bacteria and fungi promote plant growth, e.g. nitrogen fixers and mycorrhizae.
Intensive farming, with heavy use of artificial fertiliser and pesticides, frequent ploughing and compaction, can reduce soil microbial diversity.

Practices such as adding manure or compost, growing clover, reduced ploughing and crop rotation support soil microbial diversity. There is more on this in Ethics and sustainability of nutrient cycling.

notes.h: Climate warming: faster decomposition and a feedback loop
notes.b: Soil microorganisms respire faster when it is warmer. Because soils hold so much carbon, this can feed back into climate warming.
points: A rise in temperature speeds up the enzyme-controlled respiration of soil microorganisms, up to their optimum (the temperature at which their enzymes work best), so they decompose soil organic matter faster and release more CO₂.
Long-term field experiments have measured extra loss of soil carbon as CO₂ from warmed plots: forest soil plots are warmed by buried heating cables and compared with unheated plots.
Soils store more carbon than the atmosphere and all plants together, so even a small proportional loss matters.
Extra CO₂ released by warming adds to the greenhouse effect, which causes more warming, which speeds decomposition further.
This positive feedback (a change that drives more of the same change) is a major uncertainty in climate predictions.
notes.tip: Warming speeds decomposition only up to the enzymes' optimum, and drought slows microbial activity. Set out the feedback loop in order: warming, faster decomposition, more CO₂, more warming.

notes.h: Climate warming: permafrost and peat bogs
notes.b: Two kinds of waterlogged or frozen ground hold carbon that microorganisms can't normally break down. Warming can release it.
points: In the Arctic, frozen soils, called permafrost, store huge amounts of undecomposed organic matter.
As permafrost thaws, microorganisms decompose this matter, releasing CO₂ and, in waterlogged thawed soil, methane, a more powerful greenhouse gas.
Irish bogs store carbon as peat, because waterlogging stops decomposition.
Warmer, drier summers, and draining, lower the water table and let air in, so aerobic microorganisms decompose the peat and release CO₂.
Warmer waterlogged peat also releases more methane. There is more on this in Climate change and biological strategies.

notes.h: Climate warming: nitrogen, drought and uncertainty
notes.b: Warming and drought also change nutrient cycling and which microorganisms dominate. How big the long-term effect will be is still being researched.
points: Warming can speed up the release of ammonium and nitrate, giving plants more nutrients in the short term but causing more leaching (washing out by water) of nitrate.
Warming can also increase the nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas, released by nitrifying and denitrifying bacteria.
Drought reduces microbial activity, and rewetting dry soil causes a sudden burst of CO₂ release.
Warming and drought change which species dominate, e.g. the balance of bacteria and fungi, which can change how fast nutrients are cycled.
In some long-term experiments the extra CO₂ release declined after some years, because the easily decomposed carbon was used up or the microbial community adjusted (acclimatised).
How large the long-term feedback will be is still being researched.

notes.h: Investigation: soil microbial activity at different temperatures
notes.b: Aim: to show that soil microorganisms release CO₂ by respiration, and that they do so faster when warmer.
points: Independent variable: temperature, e.g. 5 °C, 15 °C and 25 °C. The dependent variable is the time the indicator takes to change colour. Equal masses of the same fresh soil keep other variables constant.
1. Put equal masses, e.g. 20 g, of the same fresh soil into sealed containers, each with a small open tube of hydrogencarbonate indicator (or limewater) suspended above the soil, not touching it.
2. Set up a control with the same mass of soil that has been sterilised by heating in an oven, so its microorganisms are dead.
3. Keep sets at different temperatures, e.g. 5 °C, 15 °C and 25 °C, in the dark.
4. Record the time for the indicator to change from red to yellow (more CO₂), or for the limewater to turn milky.
Expected result: the colour changes fastest at the highest temperature, and not, or very little, in the sterilised control. The control shows the CO₂ comes from living microorganisms.
Keep the apparatus in the dark, so that no photosynthesis by algae or seedlings removes CO₂.
Safety: wash hands after handling soil.
notes.tip: In the sterilised control the microorganisms are dead, so little or no colour change is expected. That is what links the CO₂ to living microorganisms.

notes.h: Hydrogencarbonate indicator and secondary data on microbiomes
notes.b: Two skills matter for microbiome questions: reading the CO₂ indicator, and judging published studies.
points: Hydrogencarbonate indicator colours: red (orange-red) at normal air CO₂ levels, yellow when CO₂ rises, and purple when CO₂ falls.

Secondary data to explore include published results of microbiome sequencing studies, e.g. comparisons of the gut microbiomes of people on different diets, or of babies born vaginally and by caesarean section.
Long-term soil-warming experiments and soil carbon measurements are also secondary data to explore.
When evaluating these data, check the sample size, whether the study was in humans or animals, and whether it shows correlation or cause. There is more on this in Evaluating evidence.

keyTerms.definition: The whole community of microorganisms living together in a particular environment, with their genes and the products they make.
The microorganisms themselves that make up a microbiome.
A microorganism that lives in or on a host without harming it.
A microorganism that lives with a host to the benefit of both.
An imbalance in the microbiome, such as a loss of diversity or overgrowth of harmful microorganisms.
Acids such as acetate, propionate and butyrate, produced when gut bacteria ferment fibre.
Protection against pathogens provided by the normal microbiota, which occupy attachment sites and use up nutrients.
An antibacterial protein made by some bacteria that kills competing bacteria.
The placing of gut microorganisms from a healthy donor into a patient's gut to restore a healthy microbiome.
A type of T cell, also called a regulatory T cell, that damps down inflammation.
Healthy body mass, blood glucose, blood fats and blood pressure, without obesity or type 2 diabetes.
A live microorganism taken in food or supplements to benefit health.
A food component that humans cannot digest but that feeds beneficial gut bacteria.
Stable organic matter in soil, formed from dead matter, that stores carbon for many years.
A crumb of soil particles bound together by fungal hyphae and bacterial polysaccharides, with air spaces between them.
Permanently frozen soil that stores large amounts of undecomposed organic matter.
A process in which the effect of a change increases the change itself, e.g. warming releasing CO₂ that causes more warming.
An indicator that is red at normal air CO₂ levels, yellow when CO₂ rises and purple when CO₂ falls.

questions.prompt: What is meant by a microbiome? Give two ways in which the gut microbiome benefits human health.
questions.model: A microbiome is the whole community of microorganisms living together in a particular environment, together with their genes and the products they make. Two benefits of the gut microbiome: it ferments dietary fibre to short-chain fatty acids, such as butyrate, which is the main energy source of the cells lining the colon; it makes vitamin K, needed for blood clotting. Other valid benefits: its microorganisms compete with pathogens and occupy attachment sites, providing colonisation resistance; and its molecules help train the immune system.

questions.prompt: Explain how soil microbiomes are involved in the cycling of carbon and nitrogen, and explain how climate warming could affect the carbon stored in soils.
questions.model: Carbon: bacteria and fungi decompose dead plants, animals and dung, respiring the organic carbon and releasing CO₂; part of the dead matter becomes stable humus, which stores carbon in the soil. Nitrogen: decomposers release ammonium from proteins, nitrogen-fixing bacteria add nitrogen from the air, nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate, and denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate back to nitrogen gas. Climate warming speeds up the enzyme-controlled respiration of soil microorganisms, so they decompose soil organic matter faster and release more CO₂; for example, permafrost thaws and its stored organic matter is decomposed, releasing CO₂ and methane. The extra CO₂ adds to the greenhouse effect, causing more warming, which speeds decomposition further: a positive feedback.

questions.prompt: Explore the role of the gut microbiome in immune signalling and metabolic health, and evaluate the evidence that the microbiome affects health.
questions.model: Immune signalling: molecules from gut microorganisms, such as parts of their cell walls and butyrate, are detected by immune cells in the gut lining, which send signals; butyrate promotes suppressor T cells that damp down inflammation, and this trains the immune system to tolerate harmless microorganisms and food. Metabolic health: more efficient fermentation of fibre releases more energy as SCFAs, which affect appetite hormones and how the body stores fat and controls blood glucose; inflammation from a leaky gut barrier is linked to insulin resistance. Evidence: antibiotics that disrupt the microbiome can allow Clostridioides difficile to cause severe diarrhoea; germ-free mice have poorly developed gut immune tissue; in a 2006 study, germ-free mice given microorganisms from obese mice gained more body fat than those given microorganisms from lean mice. Limits: the links in humans, such as those with obesity, type 2 diabetes, allergies and asthma, are mostly correlations, and it is often not known whether the altered microbiome causes the disease or results from it.
